title: Butterfly lace shawl
subtitle: A triangular shawl with a butterfly stitch repeat border in fingering weight.
excerpt: The butterfly stitch clusters open and close like wings across the border of this triangular shawl. The body is simple mesh; the border is where the stitch really shines, worked in rows of gathered loop clusters.
sourceNotes: Butterfly stitch construction draws on gathered-loop techniques present in mid-20th-century American crochet pattern booklets (public domain, pre-1928 editions held at Internet Archive). Triangular shaping and border placement are original to Homemade.

glossaryTerms.definition: A crochet stitch made by working multiple long loops across several rows and then gathering them with a slip stitch or chain, creating a shape that resembles butterfly wings.
A slip stitch or chain pulled through a set of long loops to cinch them together at their midpoint, forming the body of the butterfly cluster.
A simple open fabric of chain spaces and double crochet or treble stitches worked in a regular grid, forming the background of many lace shawl patterns.
Wetting the finished shawl and pinning it to open the lace and set the butterfly shapes before drying.

content.text: A butterfly lace shawl is a triangle worked from the top down. The body uses a simple
lace mesh
ground of chains and trebles; the border is six rows of
butterfly stitch
clusters that give the lower edge its character. The finished piece is 150 cm across and 70 cm deep at centre back, blocked.
The butterfly stitch works by first making long loops across four mesh rows, then using a
gathering stitch

to pull them into the wing shape. The gathered point sits at the centre of what becomes the butterfly body. The technique looks complicated but has only two moves: long yarn-overs and one pull-through.
What you need

items.name: Fingering weight yarn
items.substitutions: A smooth fingering in wool or cotton shows the butterfly cluster shapes clearly.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 12 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering weight mesh with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. The butterfly border is deeper than the mesh gauge suggests; work a 6-row butterfly swatch to check the border depth before committing to the full shawl.
Stitches used
ch: chain
sl st: slip stitch
dc (UK): double crochet
tr (UK): treble
Butterfly stitch cluster
: five long loops dropped across four rows, gathered at row 4 with one pulling sl st
Shawl body
Foundation: ch 5. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into 5th ch from hook (centre spine set). Turn.

Increase row: Ch 4 (counts as tr, ch 1). 1 tr into first tr. Work across in tr-ch-1 mesh to spine space. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine. Continue in mesh to end. Work (1 tr, ch 1, 1 tr) into turning chain. Turn.
Repeat the increase row until the shawl is 60 cm deep from the spine, measured straight down. At this point there are approximately 200 stitches across the bottom edge.
Butterfly border: 6 rows

Row 1 (right side): Work in tr-ch-1 mesh across, increasing at spine as usual. On every 8th stitch position, pull up a long loop (10 cm) instead of completing the tr. Leave the loop on the hook. Continue across. Turn. (The long loops sit loose on the hook; do not work them yet.)
Rows 2 and 3: Work in plain mesh across, letting the long loops hang at the front of the fabric. Do not work into them.
Row 4 (gathering row): Work in mesh to the first long-loop position. Insert hook through all five long loops from rows 1-3. Pull yarn through all loops in one movement (
gathering stitch
made, butterfly body formed). Continue in mesh to next long-loop position. Repeat across. Turn.
Rows 5 and 6: Work two plain mesh rows to anchor the butterfly bases.
Border edge
After Row 6, work one final row of dc (UK) along the bottom edge only, placing 1 dc into each stitch and 2 dc into each chain space. Fasten off.
Blocking
Soak, pin wingspan corners to 150 cm apart and centre back to 70 cm deep. Ease the
blocking
pins between each butterfly cluster so the wings spread open. Leave to dry completely.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: Butterfly stitch shawls have a few distinctive issues.

items.cause: Not anchoring the loop base before rows 2-3
items.fix: Place a removable stitch marker through each long loop at the base to hold its position until the gathering row.
Before gathering, fold the five loops so their midpoints align, then insert the hook and pull through all at once.
Work the butterfly rows on a hook one size larger than the body rows and return to the smaller hook for the dc border.
